claims.text: Conventionally powder-sintered single-phase ZrB2 requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally prepared ZrB2 typically has a coarser grain size.
Conventionally prepared ZrB2 typically contains residual porosity.
Residual porosity in conventionally prepared ZrB2 makes it vulnerable to liquid-induced degradation.
A liquid-phase precursor route using molecularly mixed zirconium and boron precursors can produce ZrB2 that is densified at approximately 1800 °C.
Switching to a liquid-phase precursor route will lower the required sintering temperature for single-phase ZrB2.
The liquid-phase precursor route will form ultrafine ZrB2 grains.
The liquid-phase precursor route will produce a uniformly distributed ZrB2 microstructure.
The liquid-phase precursor route will leave fewer residual pores in ZrB2.
A transient low-melting phase may form at sintering boundaries and aid pore elimination.
The liquid precursor method enables molecular-level mixing of zirconium and boron sources.
Molecular-level mixing reduces the diffusion distances required for ZrB2 formation.
Reduced diffusion distances promote ZrB2 densification at lower temperature.
A denser and more uniform ZrB2 microstructure will resist infiltration by and corrosive attack from a liquid plating bath.
Resistance to bath infiltration and corrosion will reduce hole formation and associated component failure.
Liquid-precursor-synthesized ZrB2 will have similar or better mechanical strength than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Liquid-precursor-synthesized ZrB2 will have significantly reduced porosity relative to conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Liquid-precursor-synthesized ZrB2 will have enhanced resistance to liquid-induced degradation during extended exposure.
Prior work demonstrated liquid-precursor synthesis of ultrafine single-phase high-entropy diboride powders at 1800 °C.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits mechanical strength that is merely similar to the baseline, whereas the falsification rule requires a statistically significant improvement in mechanical strength. Thus an equal-strength result could satisfy the prediction but contribute to falsification under the stated rule.
